chunks: What is an oscilloscope?. The question: What is an oscilloscope?
An oscilloscope plots voltage against time. Time runs left to right and voltage runs up and down, and the picture redraws continuously. A multimeter gives one averaged number.
A scope shows the shape of the signal, such as ripple, glitches, edges and the delay between two signals.
Compare a single average blood-pressure number with a heart monitor. The number says "normal".
The monitor draws a trace over time, so you see each beat, a skipped beat, or a sudden spike. A scope does that for a circuit's voltage.
One difference: a scope's probe becomes part of the circuit being measured.
All three have a mean of 1. 65 volts, so a DC voltmeter shows the same number for each.
Only the scope tells them apart, and the difference is exactly what will make a design work or fail.
Probe: the lead that connects the circuit to the scope input. It adds its own capacitance and affects what you see.
Volts/div and time/div: how much voltage and how much time each grid square of the screen represents. Bandwidth: the fastest signal the scope can show without rounding it off.
Trigger: the rule that decides where on the signal the picture starts, so repeating waveforms sit still.
Sample rate: how many measurements per second the scope takes to draw the trace.
Look at two signals. One is a steady 1. 65 volts. The other is a 3. 3 volts square wave that is high half the time and low half the time. A multimeter reads about 1.
65 volts for both, because their averages match. A scope shows right away that one is flat and the other jumps between 0 volts and 3. 3 volts.
Reading the screen: suppose one full cycle spans 4. 0 divisions at 50 microseconds per division. The period is 4.
0 times 50 micro s equals 200 micro s , so the frequency is 1 over 200 micro s equals 5 kilohertz. That is the whole idea.
"An oscilloscope plots voltage versus time, so instead of one number like a multimeter I see the actual waveform: edges, ripple, ringing, glitches, timing between signals.
The specs that matter are bandwidth, sample rate, memory depth, vertical resolution and channel count. Modern ones sample the input with an ADC and store it.
I always remember that the probe loads the circuit and the scope's bandwidth limits what I can see, so I choose both to fit the signal."
